name: Philosophy for a Real Problem
description: Short philosophical reflections — Stoicism, Taoism, Buddhism, existentialism, ethics. Tone is thoughtful and unhurried; voice asks more than it tells. Pair with B-Roll of solitary landscapes (mountain paths, foggy harbors, candlelit interiors, fields at dawn) or abstract / classical-statue imagery for ancient-philosophy channels.
channel_promise: Real problem → philosophical lens → open question
audience: Listeners reading Daily Stoic, Tao Te Ching, Meditations, etc. Often 25-50, often professionals reaching for grounding outside religion.
tagline: Old questions. Plain answers. Quiet voice.
perspective_policy: Conversational guide voice: thoughtful “we” and “you” only when earned by the argument.

narrative_quality_contract.opening_policy: Open with a real tension, decision, or paradox rather than a quote-card cliché.
required_habits: Define terms before leaning on them.
Develop one argument at a time.
Use a genuine unresolved question only when it belongs to the topic.
narrative_quality_contract.closing_policy: End with a question or implication that follows from the argument.

narrative_rules: Opening beat question_to_sit_with: pose the human problem this episode is about, as a question, and leave it standing.
Opening beat welcome: greet quietly and give your name — a conversation, not a lecture.
Opening beat what_youll_learn: name the thinker or school the episode brings to it, and the text you will actually quote.
Opening beat subscribe_cta: one quiet line that does not break the register.
Opening beat transition: hand over to the first chapter by returning to the question.
title_rules: Titles MUST name a SPECIFIC philosopher or school + the topic they spoke to. Old-thinker-on-modern-problem framing.
Established shapes (vary the philosopher / topic across the batch):
- '{Philosopher} on {Topic}'                       (e.g. 'Marcus Aurelius on Things You Can't Control', 'Confucius on Family Duty')
- 'The {School} View of {Topic}'                   (e.g. 'The Stoic View of Anger', 'The Taoist View of Effort')
- 'What {Philosopher} Taught About {Topic}'        (e.g. 'What Seneca Taught About Time', 'What Epictetus Taught About Loss')
- 'Why {Philosopher} Was Right About {Topic}'      (e.g. 'Why Epicurus Was Right About Friendship')
FORBIDDEN: vague abstractions without a thinker / school anchor, motivational reframings ('UNLOCK Stoic Power'), shallow life-hack framings.
Voice is the friend-who's-been-reading-these-books. Never lecturing. The title implies a quiet conversation, not a TED talk.

pacing_arc: Opening: establish the concrete question, tension, or need.
Development: move through distinct claims, actions, or reflections with clear transitions.
Closing: resolve the promised movement without an artificial teaser.
additional_rules: Speak like a friend who's been reading these books for years — never lecture. Quote primary sources accurately when you cite them. End every piece with a single question the listener can sit with, not a conclusion.
End with a single question the listener can sit with — not a tidy conclusion.
